questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with a painless, indurated ulcer on the glans penis with a clean base and raised edges. Inguinal lymph nodes are firm, non-tender and rubbery. Which test is most appropriate for initial diagnosis?
questions.exp: The description is classic for primary syphilis (Hunterian chancre). Darkfield microscopy of ulcer exudate demonstrating motile Treponema pallidum spirochetes is the gold-standard initial test. VDRL may be negative in early primary syphilis.

questions.q: A 35-year-old patient with borderline tuberculoid (BT) leprosy develops sudden erythema and tenderness along a thickened ulnar nerve with new motor weakness. Temperature is 38°C. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Increase dapsone dose and add clofazimine
Admit for surgical decompression of ulnar nerve
questions.exp: This is a Type 1 lepra reaction (reversal reaction) with acute neuritis, a dermatological emergency. High-dose corticosteroids (prednisolone 40–60 mg/day tapered over 3–6 months) are the treatment of choice to prevent irreversible nerve damage. Thalidomide is used for ENL (Type 2), not Type 1 reactions.

questions.q: A 45-year-old diabetic woman presents with a slowly expanding, red-brown indurated plaque with central clearing on her shin. Biopsy shows epithelioid granulomas with palisading histiocytes surrounding necrobiotic collagen in the dermis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Necrobiosis lipoidica (NL) classically presents on the pretibial area with yellow-brown waxy plaques and is strongly associated with diabetes mellitus. Histology shows necrobiotic collagen surrounded by palisading histiocytes in a layered pattern. Granuloma annulare lacks the characteristic yellow-brown color and epidermal atrophy seen in NL.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman develops tense blisters on normal-appearing and erythematous skin with a positive Nikolsky sign only at blister periphery. DIF shows IgG and C3 in a linear band at the dermoepidermal junction. Which antigen is targeted?
questions.exp: The clinical and DIF findings are consistent with bullous pemphigoid (BP). BP antigens are BP180 (type XVII collagen, BPAG2) and BP230 (BPAG1), both components of hemidesmosomes. Linear IgG/C3 at the BMZ on DIF is characteristic. Collagen VII is the target in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man presents with a pearly, translucent papule with telangiectatic vessels on the nose that has slowly enlarged over 2 years. The center shows slight crusting. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Nodular BCC is the most common skin malignancy and classically presents as a pearly or translucent papule/nodule with rolled edges and telangiectasias on sun-exposed areas. Keratoacanthoma grows more rapidly and has a central keratin plug. Sebaceous hyperplasia also shows central umbilication but lacks the pearly quality.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man from Bihar presents with painless depigmented macules on the trunk. Smear from a skin lesion shows abundant acid-fast bacilli. Nerve thickening is noted. What is the Ridley-Jopling classification?
questions.exp: Lepromatous leprosy (LL) has abundant bacilli (high bacterial index), multiple poorly defined lesions, diffuse infiltration, leonine facies, and nerve thickening. The host immunity is impaired (anergy). Bacteriologically positive smear with multiple lesions strongly supports LL classification.

questions.q: A 25-year-old HIV-positive man presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base along the T6 dermatome. He reports severe burning pain preceding the rash. Which antiviral drug and duration is standard of care?
opts: Acyclovir 200 mg five times/day for 5 days
Acyclovir 800 mg five times/day for 7 days
questions.exp: Herpes zoster in immunocompromised patients requires high-dose acyclovir: 800 mg five times daily for 7 days (or longer if lesions persist). Standard immunocompetent dose is also 800 mg 5 times/day for 7 days. Valacyclovir 1 g TDS for 7 days is an alternative. The 200 mg dose is for HSV, not VZV.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman has symmetrical violaceous flat-topped papules on the flexor aspects of wrists with fine white lines on the surface. Oral mucosa shows a lacy white network. Biopsy confirms the diagnosis. Which is NOT a known triggering drug for this condition?
questions.exp: Lichen planus (LP) is the diagnosis. Drug-induced LP (lichenoid drug eruption) is caused by beta-blockers, antimalarials (chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine), ACE inhibitors, thiazides, gold, and NSAIDs. Penicillin is NOT a recognized trigger. The Wickham's striae on the papule surface are pathognomonic.

questions.q: A 20-year-old student presents with itchy, erythematous, scaly plaques with sharply defined borders in the groin extending to inner thighs sparing the scrotum. KOH mount shows septate hyphae. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.exp: Tinea cruris (groin ringworm) is most commonly caused by Trichophyton rubrum, followed by Epidermophyton floccosum. Scrotal sparing distinguishes tinea cruris from candidiasis (which involves the scrotum and shows satellite lesions). T. rubrum is the most prevalent dermatophyte worldwide.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, skin thickening limited to hands, face, and forearms, telangiectasias, and calcium deposits in fingertips. ANA is positive. What antibody is most specific for her condition?
questions.exp: The clinical picture describes limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc), formerly CREST syndrome. Anti-centromere antibody (ACA) is highly specific for lcSSc (~60-80% positivity). Anti-Scl-70 is associated with diffuse cutaneous SSc and carries higher risk of pulmonary fibrosis. Anti-dsDNA is specific for SLE.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with erythema, scaling, and fissuring of the palms that worsens in winter. Potassium hydroxide preparation is negative. He has a history of psoriasis. The most appropriate treatment is:
opts: Topical clobetasol with salicylic acid and emollients
questions.exp: Palmoplantar psoriasis (keratoderma) with negative KOH is best managed with potent topical corticosteroids (clobetasol) combined with keratolytics (salicylic acid) and regular emollients. Antifungals are not indicated when KOH is negative. Mupirocin treats bacterial infections.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child develops honey-colored crusted lesions around the nose and mouth after a school epidemic. Culture grows coagulase-positive cocci. Which is the most appropriate topical treatment?
questions.exp: Non-bullous impetigo caused by Staphylococcus aureus (coagulase-positive) is most effectively treated with topical mupirocin (2% ointment/cream), which is the agent of choice for localized impetigo. Fusidic acid is an alternative. Systemic antibiotics are reserved for widespread disease or impetigo with systemic features.

questions.q: A 32-year-old sexually active woman presents with multiple painful genital ulcers with ragged, undermined edges and unilateral tender inguinal lymphadenopathy with pus discharge. Gram stain shows 'school of fish' pattern. The causative organism is:
questions.exp: The classic description with painful soft ulcers, undermined edges, and 'school of fish' pattern (gram-negative coccobacilli in chains) on Gram stain is diagnostic of chancroid caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. Syphilitic chancre is painless. LGV (Chlamydia) presents with suppurative lymphadenopathy. Donovanosis shows Donovan bodies.

questions.q: A patient undergoes patch testing for contact dermatitis. The reading at 48 hours shows erythema with papules. At 96 hours the reaction has intensified with vesicles. How is this graded according to ICDRG criteria?
questions.exp: ICDRG grading: +/- = doubtful (faint erythema only), + = weak positive (erythema, infiltration, papules), ++ = strong positive (erythema, infiltration, papules, vesicles), +++ = extreme positive (intense reaction with bullae/ulceration). The strengthening reaction with vesicles at D4 is a ++ (strong positive).

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman on long-term methotrexate for psoriasis develops fatigue and macrocytic anemia. Methotrexate dose is 15 mg weekly. Which supplementation should be given to reduce toxicity?
opts: Folic acid 5 mg daily on non-MTX days
Folinic acid (leucovorin) 15 mg weekly 24 hours after MTX
questions.exp: Folic acid 5 mg/week (on non-methotrexate days) is standard supplementation to reduce MTX-related mucositis, nausea, and megaloblastic anemia without significantly reducing efficacy. Folinic acid (leucovorin rescue) is reserved for MTX toxicity/overdose. B12 deficiency causes macrocytic anemia but is not related to MTX mechanism.

questions.q: A 55-year-old farmer presents with a painless, slowly growing, indurated nodule on the dorsum of the foot with multiple sinuses discharging sulfur granules. X-ray shows bone destruction. What is the most likely causative organism in India?
questions.exp: Mycetoma (Madura foot) in India is predominantly caused by Madurella mycetomatis (eumycetoma, fungal). This produces black granules. Actinomyces (actinomycetoma) produces white/yellow granules. Madurella mycetomatis is the most common cause of eumycetoma in India and produces black granules, is treated with azoles (itraconazole) or voriconazole.

questions.q: A 28-year-old pregnant woman (32 weeks) presents with intensely pruritic urticarial papules and plaques starting in striae of abdomen sparing the periumbilical area. DIF is negative. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy (PEP, formerly PUPPP) characteristically begins in abdominal striae in the third trimester and spares the periumbilical area. DIF is negative. Pemphigoid gestationis starts periumbilically and shows linear C3 on DIF. Cholestasis presents with pruritus without primary skin lesions (excoriations only).

questions.q: A patient with SLE develops a butterfly-shaped erythematous rash across the malar area sparing the nasolabial folds. Which UV wavelength is primarily implicated in causing photosensitivity in SLE?
questions.exp: UVB radiation (290–320 nm) is the primary trigger for photosensitivity in SLE, causing keratinocyte apoptosis and release of nuclear antigens (dsDNA, Ro/SSA), which drives the autoimmune response. However, UVA can also contribute. UVC is blocked by the ozone layer and is not relevant in clinical settings.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man presents with pigmented macules on lips and buccal mucosa since childhood, associated with multiple hamartomatous polyps of small intestine. The skin findings represent:
questions.exp: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition caused by STK11 gene mutations, characterized by mucocutaneous pigmentation (lentigines on lips, buccal mucosa, fingers) and hamartomatous gastrointestinal polyps. Addison's causes diffuse hyperpigmentation without polyps. Cronkhite-Canada is acquired with ectodermal changes.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man has a rapidly growing, dome-shaped nodule with a central keratin-filled crater on his cheek that appeared over 6 weeks. It is now beginning to involute. The most appropriate initial management is:
questions.exp: Keratoacanthoma (KA) is a rapidly growing, self-involuting squamous lesion. However, it cannot be reliably distinguished from well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma clinically or even histologically. Excision biopsy provides both diagnosis and treatment, is the standard of care, and provides a complete specimen for pathology. 'Watch and wait' risks missing SCC.

questions.q: A 16-year-old boy has acne vulgaris with inflammatory papules and pustules. He is started on doxycycline 100 mg daily. After 2 months, lesions persist. Which antibiotic-resistance mechanism is most commonly responsible for doxycycline resistance in Cutibacterium acnes?
questions.exp: Resistance to tetracyclines (including doxycycline) in Cutibacterium acnes primarily occurs due to mutations in the 16S rRNA gene (ribosomal protection) and also via tet(M) genes encoding ribosomal protection proteins. These prevent tetracycline binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit. Beta-lactamase is not a significant mechanism for tetracyclines.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man presents with annular erythematous plaques with raised, violaceous borders and central hypopigmentation on the buttocks. Histology shows dense lymphocytic infiltrate in upper dermis with epidermotropism and Pautrier microabscesses. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Mycosis fungoides (MF), the most common cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, presents with patch/plaque/tumour stages. Pautrier microabscesses (collections of atypical T-cells in epidermis) are pathognomonic. The classical sequence is patches → plaques → tumours. Epidermotropism of atypical cerebriform lymphocytes is the key histological finding.

questions.q: During liquid nitrogen cryotherapy for warts, what is the mechanism by which tissue destruction occurs?
opts: Protein denaturation by extreme heat generated during thaw
Ice crystal formation causing cellular disruption and vascular damage
Free radical generation leading to apoptosis
questions.exp: Cryotherapy destroys tissue through: (1) direct cell damage by intracellular ice crystal formation during freezing, (2) osmotic stress causing cell dehydration, and (3) microvascular injury during the thaw phase causing ischemic necrosis. The freeze-thaw cycle is more destructive than freeze alone, which is why a double freeze-thaw is recommended for warts.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman develops a target lesion on her palm — concentric zones of erythema, pale edema, and central dusky bulla — following a herpes simplex labialis episode. This is most consistent with:
questions.exp: Classic target lesions (3-zone pattern: dark center, pale middle ring, erythematous outer ring) triggered by HSV in a young patient with limited distribution (acral) and absent or minimal mucosal involvement is Erythema multiforme minor. EM major has mucosal involvement. SJS shows atypical targets (flat, 2-zone) with >2 mucosal sites and systemic toxicity.

questions.q: A 60-year-old woman presents with hypopigmented, atrophic macules with a 'cigarette paper' wrinkling on the vulva. Biopsy shows homogenized collagen in upper dermis with a lymphocytic band beneath. The diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Lichen sclerosus (LS) classically affects anogenital skin in postmenopausal women with ivory-white plaques showing 'cigarette paper' wrinkling, purpura, and 'figure-of-eight' distribution around vulva and perianal skin. Histology shows orthokeratosis, epidermal atrophy, homogenized collagen in upper dermis, and deep lymphocytic infiltrate. Associated with squamous cell carcinoma risk.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of edema of lips, tongue, and eyelids lasting 24-72 hours without urticaria. His father had similar episodes. C4 level is persistently low even between attacks. C1-esterase inhibitor (C1-INH) level is reduced. The mediator responsible for angioedema attacks is:
questions.exp: Hereditary angioedema (HAE) due to C1-INH deficiency leads to uncontrolled activation of the contact system, generating bradykinin, which increases vascular permeability. The edema is bradykinin-mediated, not histamine-mediated, which explains why antihistamines and corticosteroids are ineffective. Treatment includes C1-INH concentrate, icatibant (bradykinin-B2 receptor antagonist), or tranexamic acid.

questions.q: A 48-year-old woman on isotretinoin for nodular acne requests information about pregnancy. Which statement regarding isotretinoin teratogenicity is correct?
opts: Teratogenicity is dose-dependent, so low doses are safe in first trimester
The critical period for major malformations is after week 15 of gestation
Isotretinoin is teratogenic even at low doses; contraception is mandatory for 1 month after stopping
Male patients on isotretinoin need not worry about teratogenicity through semen
questions.exp: Isotretinoin (Pregnancy category X) is a potent teratogen causing craniofacial, cardiac, thymic, and CNS defects. It is teratogenic at any dose during organogenesis (weeks 3-16 of gestation). Effective contraception must be maintained for at least 1 month after the last dose (elimination half-life ~10-20 hours; longer for 4-oxo-isotretinoin). Male fertility/teratogenicity through semen is negligible.

questions.q: A 20-year-old woman presents with diffuse hyperpigmentation of face worsening in summer, with symmetrical distribution on cheeks, upper lip, and forehead. Wood's lamp examination accentuates the pigmentation. What does this indicate about the depth of pigment?
questions.exp: Wood's lamp (365 nm UV) accentuates pigmentation in epidermal melasma because melanin in the epidermis absorbs UV efficiently. Dermal melasma does NOT accentuate under Wood's lamp. Mixed melasma shows partial accentuation. Epidermal melasma responds better to topical depigmenting agents (hydroquinone, kojic acid, azelaic acid).

questions.q: A 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has erythematous, warm, poorly demarcated swelling of the lower leg that is rapidly spreading. He is febrile and confused. CT shows gas in fascial planes. The most appropriate intervention is:
opts: Emergency surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
IV clindamycin alone to cover anaerobes
questions.exp: Gas in fascial planes with rapidly spreading infection and systemic toxicity is necrotizing fasciitis — a surgical emergency. Immediate and aggressive surgical debridement (fasciotomy/debridement) is the cornerstone of treatment, combined with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (covering gram-positives, gram-negatives, and anaerobes — e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam + clindamycin + vancomycin). Delay in surgery dramatically increases mortality.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman has heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, and proximal muscle weakness. Anti-MDA5 antibody is positive. Which systemic complication is this patient at highest risk for?
questions.exp: Anti-MDA5 (melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5) antibody-positive dermatomyositis is associated with clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis and a high risk of rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease (RP-ILD), which carries poor prognosis. Renal crisis is associated with anti-RNA polymerase III in scleroderma. Malignancy is associated with anti-TIF1-gamma antibodies.

questions.q: During dermoscopy of a melanocytic lesion, which feature is most indicative of melanoma rather than a benign nevus?
opts: Regular pigment network with symmetric distribution
Blue-white veil with irregular streaks and regression structures
Comma-shaped vessels in a symmetric lesion
Multiple milia-like cysts with comedo-like openings
questions.exp: Blue-white veil (diffuse blue-white discoloration over an area of raised confluent hyperpigmentation), combined with irregular streaks (pseudopods/radial streaming) and regression structures (white scar-like areas or blue pepper-like granules), are major dermoscopic criteria for melanoma. Regular pigment network suggests a benign nevus. Milia-like cysts and comedo openings indicate seborrheic keratosis.
